direction: each case's query protein is searched against Swiss-Prot. Table 1 searches the other way: human proteins against one relative's proteome.

1.title: Shared ancestor, same job
1.right: a call that names the other protein's family and carries its job across
1.words: The two proteins descend from one ancestral protein and still do the same job. A call is right when it names the target's family and transfers its function.

2.title: Shared ancestor, new job
2.right: a call that names the family only; carrying the job across is a wrong label
2.words: The two proteins descend from one ancestral protein, but the query protein has taken on a different job. A call is right when it names the family, and wrong when it carries the target's function across.

3.title: No shared ancestor, whole protein
3.right: a call that points at a protein doing the same job; naming a shared family is wrong, because the two have no common ancestor
3.words: The two proteins reached the same job from different ancestors, so there is no family truth. A call that names a family shared with the other protein is wrong, even though it points at a protein that does the same job; the card marks it wrong label and says what the call did get right.

4.title: No shared ancestor, short motif
4.right: a call that covers the right few residues
4.words: A short stretch of the query protein copies a short stretch of a human protein. A call is right when it lands on those residues.

result_words.found: a call on the right target, overlapping the truth region with an IoU of 0.5 or more
result_words.wrong place: a call on the right target, overlapping the truth region with an IoU below 0.5
result_words.wrong label: the call carries the human protein's function to a protein that does not have it
result_words.missed: no call on the target above the tool's own cutoff
result_words.not run: the search has not been run yet; the card says why

cases.name: CED-9 against BCL-2
cases.experiment: Human bcl-2 put into C. elegans stopped the programmed cell death that loss of ced-9 causes, and ced-9 itself carries the same activity.
cases.takeaway: Two proteins that do the same job can sit near the edge of what a sequence search reports. A weak hit to a protein of the right family is worth reading, not throwing away.
cases.earlier_runs: An earlier search of CED-9 against the human GENCODE v49 canonical proteome is stored in seanome/2024-kmerseek-analysis, branch olgabot/case-gallery-reference-pairs, commit 3e3767c1, files tables/case_gallery/other_tools/*.tsv. phmmer puts CED-9 residues 111 to 232 on BCL-2 residues 68 to 235, E = 7.9e-05. jackhmmer puts 100 to 229 on 73 to 208, E = 7.7e-41. MMseqs2 with three rounds puts 101 to 236 on 82 to 211, E = 8.1e-20, and with one round reports no BCL-2 row at all. Those runs had no decoy and searched a different database, so they are not in the table above.

cases.name: A bacterial TIR-domain protein against the TIR domain of TLR4
cases.experiment: Purified TirS cleaves NAD, and the full-length protein lowers NAD in human cells, which the catalytically dead E216A protein does not. The TIR domain of TLR4 holds a signalling complex together and does no such chemistry, which is what puts this pair in box 2. The one human TIR domain that does cleave NAD, SARM1, would put the same bacterial protein in box 1.
cases.takeaway: A domain shared between a bacterium and a human can carry a different job in each. The safe transfer is the domain name, not the human protein's role.
cases.wrong_label: holds a Toll-like receptor signalling complex together

cases.experiment: P66 binds the human receptor SIRPα, the receptor CD47 binds, and Borrelia lacking P66 is taken up by macrophages more readily.

Foldseek on the two AlphaFold models gives one hit, E = 3.047, bit score 3, over 22 aligned residues (seanome/2024-kmerseek-analysis notebook 276, commit 7043bd98). Those runs had no decoy and searched a different database.

cases.name: Antifreeze glycoprotein, Antarctic notothenioid against Arctic cod
cases.experiment: Both fish make the same ice-binding glycoprotein from a repeat of the same three residues. The notothenioid gene came from a trypsinogen and the cod gene did not, and the two genes differ in their introns, spacers and codon use.
cases.takeaway: Two fish lineages arrived at the same repeated glycoprotein from different genes, so a strong sequence match is not by itself evidence of common ancestry.
cases.target_rule: The Arctic cod protein is the longest of the Boreogadus saida antifreeze glycoprotein polypeptides in UniProt, so that its length is closest to the notothenioid polyprotein's. The two match closely because both are a repeat of the same three residues, which is what the paper calls convergent, not inherited.

alignment.source: best local alignment of the two sequences, BLOSUM62, gap open 11, gap extend 1, computed by scripts/known_cases.py

cases.name: Influenza A NS1 against the histone H3 tail
cases.experiment: The last residues of NS1 copy the start of the histone H3 tail. NS1 binds the human PAF1 transcription complex through them, and changing them ends the binding.
cases.takeaway: Four residues are shorter than the shortest word any of these tools indexes. Every search here is expected to be silent, and a motif scanner is the right tool.

structure.what: the NS1 C-terminal tail, 15 residues, bound to the CHD1 chromodomains, 1.87 Å. That structure is reported by a later paper, Qin et al., Nature Communications 5 (2014): 3952, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms4952, not by reference 14

cases.structure_note: The only experimental structure of this stretch holds 15 residues of NS1, not the whole protein, and it is the tail of a different H3N2 strain (UniProt Q38SQ2).
cases.motif_note: UniProt numbers the histone from its initial methionine, so the ARTK of the H3 tail is residues 2 to 5 there and residues 1 to 4 in the chromatin literature.

alignment.source: the motif with 1 residue before it and 6 after, as many as both proteins have, set side by side

cases.name: Ten pathogen motifs from ELM against their human partners
cases.experiment: Each instance is a short motif in a virus or bacterial protein. The Eukaryotic Linear Motif resource records the experiments that showed it binds a human protein.
cases.takeaway: Short pathogen motifs are the part of annotation these nine tools are least suited to. That is why the leaderboard reports region length as its own axis.
cases.pick_rule: The ten ELM instances with the lowest ELM instance identifiers that meet all of: the protein is from a virus or a bacterium by its UniProt lineage; ELM records the instance as experimentally shown (its "true positive" status); and ELM records a binding partner that is a human protein, at the same motif coordinates. The rule was fixed before any search was run; scripts/known_cases_elm.py applies it.

alignment.source: best local alignment of the two sequences, BLOSUM62, gap open 11, gap extend 1, computed by scripts/known_cases.py
